questions.q: What is ECMAScript?
questions.explain: Ecma International publishes the ECMAScript standard; every engine implements it. "JavaScript" is the everyday name for the language that standard describes.
options: An older language that JavaScript replaced
The official standard (ECMA-262) that describes the JavaScript language
A framework for building web pages

questions.q: A tutorial says "this needs ES6". Which edition is that?
questions.explain: ES6 is the old name of ES2015, the big update that brought let, const, arrow functions, classes, modules and promises. From then on, editions are named after their year.

questions.q: Why has a new ECMAScript edition come out every year since 2016?
questions.explain: After the six-year gap before ES2015, TC39 moved to a "release train": each June, the finished features ship, and anything not ready waits for the next year.
options: Because browsers are updated once a year
Because big releases years apart (and the abandoned ES4) were slow and risky; a yearly release ships whatever is finished
Because old features are removed every year
Because the standard expires after twelve months

questions.q: A blog post shows a proposal "currently at stage 2". What does that tell you?
questions.explain: Only stage 4 means finished and part of the language. At stage 2 the specification is a draft, so the feature, and the blog post about it, may change.
options: It is part of JavaScript and safe everywhere
A design has been chosen, but details can still change: do not rely on it in production
It works in exactly two browsers

questions.q: What does stage 3 mean for a proposal?
questions.explain: Stage 3 is "ready to implement". It reaches stage 4 after it passes the Test262 suite and ships in at least two engines.
options: The committee has just agreed the problem is worth solving
The design is finished and engines are asked to implement it; only problems found while implementing can change it
It is in the next June edition
It is waiting for a name

questions.q: How does TC39 decide to move a proposal forward?
questions.explain: TC39 works by consensus, and its proposals and meeting notes are public on GitHub.
options: By a majority vote of browser makers
By consensus: it moves only when no member objects
By a public poll of developers

questions.q: Why will typeof null always be "object", although everyone agrees it is a mistake?
questions.explain: "Don't break the web" is TC39's first rule. Billions of pages will never be updated, so a behaviour, once shipped, almost never changes.
options: Because fixing it would break existing websites that rely on the old behaviour, and the web must keep working
Because it was fixed in ES2015 but browsers ignore the fix

questions.q: Why is the array method called flat() and not flatten()?
questions.explain: In 2018 the proposal was renamed so that pages using MooTools kept working. It is a real example of "don't break the web".
options: Because an old library (MooTools) had added its own, different flatten, and the new one would have broken sites using it
Because Safari already had a flatten method

questions.q: Where does console.log come from?
questions.explain: The engine runs the language; the host adds abilities such as printing, timers and networking. Browsers and Node.js both provide console, following a separate standard.
options: It is part of the ECMAScript standard
The host (the browser or Node.js) provides it; it is not part of ECMAScript itself
From an npm package installed with Node.js

questions.q: Why is typeof document equal to "undefined" in Node.js?
questions.explain: The language is the same; the host differs. The browser adds document and window; Node.js adds process and file access instead.
options: Because Node.js runs an older version of JavaScript
Because document is the web page, provided by the browser host, and a server has no page
Because Node.js does not support objects

questions.q: You want to use a feature added in ES2025. Why is the decision easier for backend code than for code sent to browsers?
questions.explain: Check your server's Node.js version once and you know. For browsers you must check compatibility tables (MDN, caniuse.com), detect features, or transpile.
options: Backend code does not use ECMAScript
On the server you choose the Node.js version; in browsers, your visitors' devices decide

questions.q: Which line checks whether Object.groupBy exists without crashing on an older runtime?
questions.explain: typeof gives "undefined" for a missing property instead of throwing, so this is feature detection. Calling a missing method throws a TypeError.

questions.q: What is the difference between a transpiler and a polyfill?
questions.explain: New syntax (like ?.) cannot be added by a function, so a tool must rewrite it. A missing function (like Object.groupBy) can be added by code: that is a polyfill.
options: They are two names for the same tool
A transpiler rewrites new syntax into older syntax; a polyfill adds a missing built-in function written in older JavaScript
A transpiler runs in the browser; a polyfill runs on the server

questions.q: Which engine does Node.js use?
questions.explain: Node.js is built on V8, the engine from Chrome. SpiderMonkey is Firefox's engine and JavaScriptCore is Safari's (and Bun's).

questions.q: Which of these is an expression?
questions.explain: An expression produces a value. price * quantity does; a declaration, an if and a for are statements that do something but produce no value you can use.

questions.q: Which of these can go inside ${…} in a template literal?
questions.explain: Only expressions fit in ${…}. The ternary operator is the expression form of if/else, which is why it is used there.

questions.q: A function ends with return on one line and the object it should return on the next line. What does it return?
questions.explain: A line break is not allowed directly after return, so automatic semicolon insertion ends the statement there. Start the returned value on the same line: return {.
options: undefined, because a semicolon is inserted right after return

questions.q: In code written without semicolons, a line starting with which character can silently join the line before it?
questions.explain: A line starting with (, [ or a backtick can continue the previous expression (as a call, an index or a tagged template), so no semicolon is inserted.
options: / at the start of a // comment

questions.q: You wrap some code in /* … */ to disable it, but the code already contains a /* note */ comment. What happens?
questions.explain: Block comments do not nest. Disable lines with // in front of each one instead; editors do this with one shortcut.
options: The first */ ends your comment early, and the rest is read as code, usually a syntax error

questions.q: By convention, which name is most likely a class you create with new?
questions.explain: PascalCase marks classes and constructors (Map, Date, BankAccount). camelCase is for variables and functions, UPPER_SNAKE_CASE for fixed settings, and dashes are not allowed in names at all.

questions.q: Which is the best name for a boolean that says whether an invoice has been paid?
questions.explain: Boolean names read as yes/no questions: isPaid, hasStock, canWithdraw. paidAmount suggests a number.

questions.q: In an ES module, you mistype a variable: totl = 5000 instead of total = 5000. What happens?
questions.explain: Strict mode turns assignment to an undeclared name into an error. Every ES module is strict automatically, so typos like this are caught at once.
options: A new global variable totl is created silently
A ReferenceError, because modules are always in strict mode

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A semicolon is inserted right after return, so the function returns nothing. The sum on the next line is never evaluated.

questions.q: Without a semicolon, the second line joins the first. What does this print?
questions.explain: The engine reads const city = "Lagos"[1, 2]. Inside the brackets, 1, 2 evaluates to 2, so city is the character at position 2 of "Lagos": "g".

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The line starting with ( continues the previous one, so the engine reads fee(2 + 3): a call to a number, which throws a TypeError at run time.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A line break is not allowed before a postfix ++, so a semicolon goes after orders and the ++ attaches to the next line: orders; ++refunds;.
questions.code:
let orders = 1
let refunds = 1
orders
++
refunds
console.log(orders, refunds)

questions.q: What does this print, in both Node.js and the browser?
questions.explain: Math is a built-in object; JSON.stringify and console.log are functions. typeof on a name that does not exist gives "undefined" instead of throwing, which is what makes feature detection safe.
questions.code: console.log(typeof Math, typeof JSON.stringify, typeof console.log, typeof notDefinedAnywhere);

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: flat() joins the inner lists into one list of 4 places. flatten does not exist: it was renamed to flat so that old websites would not break.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: new Function(code) only compiles the text; it does not run it, so nothing is printed by the first one except "valid". An if statement where a value is expected is a syntax error.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: * runs before +, as in school maths, so the first is 8500 + 5000. Parentheses change the order: 8502 × 2500.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A ternary is an expression, so it fits in ${…} and can be chained: 25,000 is not under 10,000, but it is under 50,000.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Whitespace between tokens does not matter to the engine, so the odd layout still works. Inside a string, spaces are part of the text: " x " has 3 characters.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: prise was never declared. In strict mode assigning to it throws a ReferenceError instead of silently creating a global variable, so the typo is caught.

questions.q: This function returns undefined instead of the receipt. Fix it without changing what the receipt contains.
questions.explain: The returned value must start on the same line as return; otherwise a semicolon is inserted after return.

questions.q: This program should print the two branch names and then the shop name. Add the missing semicolons so the lines stay separate.
questions.explain: Without a semicolon, the line starting with [ continues branches[0] as another index and the program crashes. Ending every statement with ; removes the ambiguity.
questions.starter:
const shop = "Mama Titi"
const branches = ["Ikeja", "Yaba"]
const first = branches[0]
[first, branches[1]].forEach((b) => console.log(b))
console.log(shop)

questions.q: Finish the template literal so it prints Order ORD-7: paid when isPaid is true and Order ORD-7: awaiting payment otherwise. Use a ternary inside ${…}.
questions.explain: ${…} only accepts an expression, so an if statement cannot go there; the ternary is the expression form of a choice.
questions.expected:
Order ORD-7: paid
Order ORD-7: awaiting payment

questions.q: Write supports(owner, name) that returns true when owner[name] is a function, using typeof, so it never crashes on a missing feature.
questions.explain: Reading a missing property gives undefined, and typeof undefined is "undefined", so the check is safe. This is feature detection.

questions.q: Strict mode caught a typo in this function: it prints a ReferenceError. Fix the typo so the function returns the total with delivery.
questions.explain: In strict mode, assigning to the undeclared totl throws instead of quietly creating a new global variable, which is how the typo was found.

questions.q: Print a receipt with three lines: the rice line (Rice x1 8500), the oil line (Oil x2 5000, where 5000 is computed as 2 * 2500) and TOTAL 13500, computed from the two amounts in one expression.
questions.explain: console.log prints its arguments separated by spaces. Each argument is an expression, so the engine computes 2 * 2500 and 8500 + 2 * 2500 (multiplication first) before printing.
questions.starter:
console.log("Rice x1", 8500);
// print the oil line and the total

questions.q: Someone disabled the discount with a block comment around code that already contains a comment, and now the program will not run. Disable the discount line correctly with // so that the program prints 13500.
questions.explain: Block comments do not nest: the first */ ended the outer comment and the final */ became broken code. A line comment hides everything to the end of its line, including the inner block comment.

questions.q: Write kindOf(names) that returns a string listing each name and its typeof on globalThis, like Math:object, joined by spaces. Use it on ["Math", "JSON", "setTimeout", "NotReal"].
questions.explain: globalThis holds every global name, from the language (Math, JSON) and from the host (setTimeout). A missing name reads as undefined without crashing.
